lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview – algorithms and data structures

scenes.text: The interviewer shares a doc and says: 'Think aloud.'
You have 2.5 minutes per question.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Restate the problem, clarify constraints, give a brute-force idea, improve it, state complexity, then test with a tiny case. The engine scores key points; compare with the model answer.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Say the complexity out loud for every approach. Interviewers listen for trade-offs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Jumping to code without clarifying.
- Ignoring edge cases (empty input, duplicates).
- Silent thinking.

activity.role: Software Engineer – algorithms and data structures

rounds.q: Given a stream of numbers, how do you maintain the k largest in memory?
points: push then pop min when size>k
O(n log k) time, O(k) space
rounds.model: I keep a min-heap of size k. For each number I push it, and if the heap exceeds k I pop the smallest, so the heap always holds the k largest seen. Time is O(n log k) and space O(k), better than sorting the entire stream when k is small and the data does not fit in memory. At the end I pop or sort the heap to output in order.
followups: How would you get the median of a stream?

rounds.q: When does Dijkstra's algorithm fail and what do you use instead?
rounds.model: Dijkstra assumes that once a vertex is popped with the smallest tentative distance, no later path can improve it; negative edges break this. Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges V−1 times, handles negative edges and can detect negative cycles with one more pass, at O(VE). For DAGs a topological-order relaxation is O(V+E).

rounds.q: Explain dynamic programming using the 0/1 knapsack.
rounds.model: DP applies when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. For knapsack, dp[i][w] is the best value using the first i items with capacity w: either skip item i or take it if it fits. That is O(nW) time, pseudo-polynomial because W is a number's value. A 1-D array works if the capacity loop runs downward so each item is used once.
followups: Why is knapsack NP-hard if it is O(nW)?

rounds.q: A hash table has O(1) average lookup. When does it degrade and how do you mitigate it?
points: tree buckets or randomised hash seeds
rounds.model: Lookup degrades towards O(n) when many keys collide, caused by a high load factor, a poor hash function or adversarial inputs. Mitigations: resize and rehash when load exceeds a threshold, use good randomised hash functions, and use balanced-tree buckets as Java's HashMap does for long chains.

rounds.q: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
rounds.model: Run DFS with three states: unvisited, in the current recursion stack, finished. Reaching a node that is in the stack is a back edge and means a cycle. Alternatively run Kahn's algorithm: if a topological order cannot include all vertices, a cycle exists. Both are O(V+E).
followups: How does it differ for undirected graphs?

tips: Clarify constraints before choosing an algorithm

sources: Original mock interview material

lessons.title: Lab: Mock interview – system design

scenes.text: The prompt: 'Design a URL shortener.'
Numbers first, then boxes and arrows.

steps.title: Framework
steps.body: Requirements → estimates → API → data model → high-level design → deep dive on bottlenecks → failure handling and monitoring → trade-offs. Always say what you would build first and what you would leave out.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body: Back-of-envelope figures justify choices such as sharding or caching.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Diving into one component too early.
- No failure discussion.
- Buzzwords without reasons.

rounds.q: Design a URL shortener for 1 billion links and 100:1 read to write ratio.
rounds.model: Requirements: create and redirect, low-latency reads, high availability. Estimate: 1B links × ~500 B ≈ 500 GB, small enough to shard simply. Generate unique IDs from a distributed counter or Snowflake IDs and encode in base62; 7 characters give 3.5 trillion codes. Store id→URL in a replicated key-value or SQL store sharded by id; put a cache (Redis) in front for hot links since reads dominate. Redirect with 302 if analytics matter. Handle abuse with validation and rate limits, and expire links with TTL.
followups: How do you avoid ID collisions across regions?

rounds.q: Your API latency suddenly doubled after a deploy. How do you investigate?
points: compare metrics before and after, scope
rounds.model: I first scope it: which endpoints, regions and percentiles, and when it started versus the deploy. If it correlates with the deploy and impact is high I roll back, then investigate. I use traces and metrics to see whether time is in the app, the database or a downstream call, check connection pools, slow queries and cache hit ratio, and reproduce in staging. Finally I write a blameless review and add an alert or test.
followups: What if it is not correlated with the deploy?

rounds.q: Explain the CAP theorem with an example design choice.
rounds.model: During a network partition a distributed store must choose between consistency (reject or delay some requests so all see the same data) and availability (answer using possibly stale data). Partitions will happen, so the real choice is C or A when they do. A bank ledger favours consistency; a social feed favours availability. Systems offer tuning through quorum sizes R and W.

rounds.q: How would you design a rate limiter for a public API?
points: failure mode if the store is down
rounds.model: I would use a token bucket per API key, stored in Redis with atomic operations so all servers share counters. It allows bursts while bounding the average rate. Rejected requests get 429 with Retry-After. If Redis is down, I would fail open with a conservative local limit rather than block all traffic, and alert.

rounds.q: How do you ensure a payment is not processed twice when clients retry?
rounds.model: The client sends a unique idempotency key. The server records the key and result in the same transaction as the charge, protected by a unique constraint; a repeat request with the same key returns the stored result without charging again. Keys expire after a window such as 24 hours.
followups: What if two requests with the same key arrive concurrently?

tips: Draw a high-level design before details

sources: Original mock interview material

lessons.title: Lab: Behavioural, ML and leadership round

scenes.text: The manager asks you to explain overfitting to a non-technical person.
Clear explanation shows maturity.

steps.title: Skills
steps.body: Translate technical ideas into plain analogies, then give numbers. Use STAR for stories: Situation, Task, Action, Result, plus what you learned. For ML questions mention data, metric, baseline and monitoring.

steps.title: Weak vs strong
steps.body: Weak: 'Accuracy is high.' Strong: 'Accuracy is 98%, but recall on the fraud class is 40%, so we tune the threshold.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Only technical jargon.
- Claiming credit for team work without saying your part.
- Fabricating results.

activity.role: Senior developer / team lead – behavioural and ML round

rounds.q: Describe a technically hard problem you solved in your major project.
rounds.model: In our MCA project, report queries took 8 seconds on 2 million rows. I profiled with EXPLAIN, found a missing composite index and an N+1 query in the API. I added the index, rewrote the query as a join and cached the result for five minutes. Latency fell to 300 ms, and I added a regression test with a load script.
followups: What did you rule out first?

rounds.q: Explain overfitting to a non-technical manager and how you prevent it.
rounds.model: Overfitting is like a student memorising last year's questions: perfect on those, poor on new ones. We detect it by checking performance on data the model never saw. We prevent it with more data, simpler models, regularisation, early stopping and cross-validation.
followups: How would you explain precision and recall?

rounds.q: A model has 98% accuracy on fraud detection where 1% of transactions are fraud. Is it good?
rounds.model: Not necessarily. A model that always predicts 'not fraud' has 99% accuracy. I would look at precision, recall and the precision–recall curve, and choose a threshold based on the cost of missing fraud versus annoying genuine customers. I would also use stratified validation and consider resampling or class weights.
followups: How do you monitor it in production?

rounds.q: Tell me about a conflict with a teammate or guide and how you resolved it.
rounds.model: A teammate and I disagreed on the framework. I proposed a short comparison against our requirements: time, skills and testing support. We agreed on the option that scored higher and documented the decision in an ADR. We shipped on time and kept working well together.
followups: What would you do if you still disagreed?

rounds.q: Where do you want to be in five years?
rounds.model: I want to be a technical lead who designs reliable systems and mentors junior engineers. In the next years I plan to deepen distributed systems and ML engineering, take ownership of production services and contribute to the team's engineering culture.
followups: Which skills will you build first?

steps.title: README
steps.body: Include: what it does, screenshot, quick start, tech stack, design decisions, how to run tests, licence.

steps.title: Review
steps.body: Ask a peer to follow the README on a clean machine.

activity.prompt: Tick each item in your final packet.

Repository with README and quick start
Unit and integration tests passing in CI
Peer followed README on a clean machine

lessons.title: Lab: Top-k with a min-heap

scenes.text: A store streams millions of sales and needs the 3 best-sellers without sorting everything.
A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest seen so far.

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: Keep a min-heap of size k. For each item, push; if size exceeds k pop the minimum. After the pass the heap holds the k largest. Time O(n log k), space O(k) — better than sorting O(n log n) when k ≪ n. Python's heapq is a min-heap.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: Stream [5,1,9,3,7,8], k=3: heap ends {7,8,9}. Sorted descending: [9,8,7].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a max-heap of size n.
- Forgetting heapq has only a min-heap (negate for max).
- Assuming the heap list is sorted.

activity.prompt: Using heapq maintain a heap of size 3 over [5,1,9,3,7,8] and print the k largest in descending order as a list.
activity.solution:
import heapq
data=[5,1,9,3,7,8]
k=3
h=[]
for x in data:
    heapq.heappush(h,x)
    if len(h)>k: heapq.heappop(h)
print(sorted(h,reverse=True))
activity.hint: Pop the smallest when size > k.

quiz.q: Complexity of top-k via heap of size k?

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: BFS shortest path in an unweighted graph

scenes.text: A city app finds the route with the fewest stops.
BFS explores level by level so the first arrival is the fewest-edge path.

steps.title: BFS
steps.body: Queue-based. Mark visited when enqueuing, store parent pointers, reconstruct the path by walking back from the target. O(V+E). BFS gives shortest paths only when all edges have equal cost; for weights use Dijkstra.

steps.title: Graph
steps.body: A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E. From A to E: A→B→D→E (3 edges).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Marking visited on dequeue (duplicates in queue).
- Using a stack (DFS) and expecting shortest paths.
- Not handling unreachable targets.

activity.prompt: Run BFS from A to E on the graph above (visit neighbours in alphabetical order) and print the path as `A B D E`.

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Dijkstra with a priority queue

scenes.text: A rider wants the cheapest route; roads have different travel times.
Dijkstra always expands the nearest unfinished vertex.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Initialise dist[source]=0, others ∞. Pop the smallest (d,u) from a min-heap; skip if stale; relax each edge (u,v,w): if d+w < dist[v], update and push. O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap. Requires non-negative weights; negative edges need Bellman–Ford.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Dijkstra with negative edges.
- Not skipping stale heap entries.
- Treating the undirected edge as one-way.

activity.prompt: Compute the shortest distance from A to D on the undirected weighted graph above and print it (4).

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – knapsack by dynamic programming

scenes.text: A trekker can carry 7 kg and must maximise value.
DP stores best value for each capacity so subproblems are solved once.

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i−1][w], dp[i−1][w−wt[i]] + val[i]) if wt[i] ≤ w else dp[i−1][w]. Use a 1-D array iterating w downward to avoid reusing an item. Time O(nW), space O(W) — pseudo-polynomial (W is a value, not input length).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Items (weight,value): (1,1),(3,4),(4,5),(5,7), capacity 7. Best: weights 3+4 for value 9. Alternatives: 5+1 → 8; 4+1 → 6; 5 alone → 7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Iterating w upward in 1-D (unbounded knapsack by mistake).
- Confusing 0/1 with fractional knapsack (greedy).
- Calling O(nW) polynomial.

activity.prompt: Solve 0/1 knapsack for weights [1,3,4,5], values [1,4,5,7], capacity 7 and print the maximum value (9).

courses.title: Advanced DBMS: Window Functions, CTEs, Transactions
courses.summary: Graduate database practicals: ranking and running totals with window functions, CTEs for top-N per group, transaction anomalies and isolation, and indexing trade-offs. Foundations: uni-cse-dbms.
outcomes: Learners can use window functions to rank and accumulate
Learners can write CTEs for top-N-per-group
Learners can explain isolation anomalies
Learners can reason about index use

lessons.title: Lab: Rank within a department

scenes.text: HR wants each employee's pay rank inside their own department.
Window functions compute per-partition values without collapsing rows.

steps.title: Syntax
steps.body: `func() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)`. RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK does not (1,1,2); ROW_NUMBER is always unique. Unlike GROUP BY, rows are preserved.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: HR: Divya 1, Bilal 2. IT: Chen 1, Asha 2. Sales: Esha 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using WHERE on a window result directly (wrap in a subquery/CTE).
- Forgetting PARTITION BY (ranks whole table).
- Mixing RANK and ROW_NUMBER semantics.

activity.prompt: Print dept, name and rank by salary (highest = 1) within each dept, ordered by dept then rank.
activity.solution: SELECT dept, name, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM emp ORDER BY dept, r;
activity.hint: PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE emp(id INT,name VARCHAR,dept VARCHAR,salary INT); INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',50000),(2,'Bilal','HR',40000),(3,'Chen','IT',60000),(4,'Divya','HR',45000),(5,'Esha','Sales',35000); CREATE TABLE orders(id INT,day INT,amt INT); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,100),(2,2,250),(3,3,50),(4,4,300);

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Running totals and moving sums

scenes.text: The owner wants cumulative sales by day.
A frame defines which rows the window sees.

steps.title: Frames
steps.body: `SUM(amt) OVER (ORDER BY day)` defaults to RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW, giving a running total. `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` gives a 3-day moving sum. LAG/LEAD fetch previous/next row values for day-over-day change.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER.
- Using RANGE where ROWS is intended with duplicate order values.
- Dividing by LAG when it is NULL.

activity.prompt: Print day and running total of amt ordered by day.
activity.solution: SELECT day, SUM(amt) OVER (ORDER BY day) FROM orders ORDER BY day;
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE emp(id INT,name VARCHAR,dept VARCHAR,salary INT); INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',50000),(2,'Bilal','HR',40000),(3,'Chen','IT',60000),(4,'Divya','HR',45000),(5,'Esha','Sales',35000); CREATE TABLE orders(id INT,day INT,amt INT); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,100),(2,2,250),(3,3,50),(4,4,300);

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Transactions and the lost update

scenes.text: Two clerks update the same account at once: balance 1000, one deposits 200, one withdraws 300.
Without isolation one update can overwrite the other.

steps.title: ACID and isolation
steps.body: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update. Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. Higher isolation = fewer anomalies, more blocking/aborts. Use row locks (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) or atomic updates (`balance = balance + 200`).

steps.title: Bad pattern
steps.body: Both read 1000; one writes 1200, other writes 700 → final 700 (the deposit is lost). Correct final is 900.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Read-modify-write in application code without locking.
- Assuming default isolation prevents everything.
- Long transactions holding locks.

a.text: Two concurrent requests update account 42 (balance 1000): +200 and −300. Which design is safest?

choices.label: Each reads the balance, computes, and writes the new value
Use UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + :delta inside a transaction
choices.feedback: The database applies both deltas atomically.

bad.text: Final balance 700 or 1200; one update vanished.

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – top earner per department with a CTE

scenes.text: The board wants the top earner in every department.
A CTE ranks first; the outer query keeps rank 1.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: `WITH ranked AS (SELECT …, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM emp) SELECT … FROM ranked WHERE rn=1`. CTEs improve readability; recursive CTEs traverse hierarchies. Indexes on (dept, salary) can help the sort, but check the plan with EXPLAIN.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: HR Divya, IT Chen, Sales Esha.

steps.title: Index thinking
steps.body: An index helps when it narrows many rows to few; on tiny tables a scan is faster. Composite index order matters: equality columns first, then range/sort.

activity.prompt: Print dept and name of the top-paid employee in each department ordered by dept.
activity.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT dept,name,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM emp) SELECT dept,name FROM ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY dept;
activity.hint: Filter rn = 1 in the outer query.
activity.setup: CREATE TABLE emp(id INT,name VARCHAR,dept VARCHAR,salary INT); INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha','IT',50000),(2,'Bilal','HR',40000),(3,'Chen','IT',60000),(4,'Divya','HR',45000),(5,'Esha','Sales',35000); CREATE TABLE orders(id INT,day INT,amt INT); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,100),(2,2,250),(3,3,50),(4,4,300);

options: Filter by dept sorted by salary

courses.title: Software Design Patterns in Python
courses.summary: Strategy, Observer and Factory patterns with runnable examples, plus a plug-in notification capstone, to design maintainable systems. Complements uni-cse-oop and uni-cse-se.
outcomes: Learners can swap behaviour with Strategy
Learners can decouple publishers and subscribers with Observer

lessons.title: Lab: Strategy – interchangeable discounts

scenes.text: A shop has student, festival and no-discount pricing rules that keep changing.
Strategy lets the rule be passed in as a parameter.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each, and make them interchangeable. In Python a function can be the strategy. Benefit: open/closed principle — add rules without editing checkout code.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: student: 10% off; festival: 25% off; none: unchanged. checkout(price, rule).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- if/elif chains that grow forever.
- Strategy objects that depend on each other.
- Over-engineering a single rule.

activity.prompt: Implement checkout(price, rule) where rule is a function; define student (10% off) and festival (25% off). Print the festival price of 800 and the student price of 500 as `600.0 450.0`.
activity.hint: Pass the function and call it.

quiz.q: In Python a strategy can be?

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Observer – notify subscribers

scenes.text: When a stock price changes, several screens must update.
The subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: Subject holds state and observers; observers register with subscribe and implement update. Loose coupling: the subject does not know concrete observer types. Used in GUIs, event buses and reactive libraries. Beware memory leaks from forgotten unsubscribes.

steps.title: Flow
steps.body: set_price(120) → every subscriber receives 120.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Observers modifying the subject during notification.
- Never unsubscribing.
- Exceptions in one observer blocking the rest.

activity.prompt: Create a Stock class with subscribe(fn) and set_price(p) that calls all subscribers. Subscribe two functions that append `A:120` and `B:120` to a list and print the list.

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Factory – create objects by name

scenes.text: The report module must export to CSV or JSON depending on a setting.
A factory hides which class is created.

steps.title: Pattern
steps.body: A factory function maps a key to a constructor, so callers do not use `if type == …` everywhere. Add a new type by registering one entry. Combine with a registry dict.

steps.title: Registry
steps.body: {'csv': CsvExporter, 'json': JsonExporter}; unknown key raises a clear ValueError.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Factories that return different shapes.
- Silent fallbacks for unknown keys.
- Factory used where a simple constructor suffices.

activity.prompt: Write make_exporter(kind) returning a function: 'csv' joins a list with commas, 'json' joins with `;`. Print make_exporter('csv')([1,2,3]) as `1,2,3`.

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – plug-in notification service

scenes.text: An alerting tool must send messages via email, SMS or chat and let new channels be added by other teams.
The design combines Factory (create channel), Strategy (how to send) and Observer (who is notified).

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Define a send(message) interface. Register channels in a factory registry. A Notifier subject keeps subscribers and calls each channel's send; failure in one channel is caught so others still run. Write tests with fake channels.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Subscribing email and sms then notifying 'disk full' produces two sent messages.

steps.title: Review
steps.body: Check coupling: adding a Slack channel should require one new class and one registry line, nothing else.

activity.prompt: Implement Notifier with subscribe(channel_fn) and notify(msg) that catches exceptions per channel. Subscribe email, a failing channel and sms; print the list of successful deliveries: ['email:disk full', 'sms:disk full'].

uni-mca-sem2.title: MCA Semester 2: Distributed Systems, ML, Containers
uni-mca-sem2.description: Second semester of MCA: distributed systems simulations, machine learning from scratch and container operations with a simulated Docker console.

courses.title: Distributed Systems Lab
courses.summary: Graduate distributed-systems practicals: logical clocks, quorums, consistent hashing and replica availability, using small deterministic simulations. Related: uni-cse-cn, uni-cse-os, uni-cse-cloud.
outcomes: Learners can assign Lamport timestamps
Learners can choose quorum sizes for consistency
Learners can place keys with consistent hashing
Learners can compute availability of replicated services

lessons.title: Lab: Lamport logical clocks

scenes.text: Messages from three servers arrive in odd orders because physical clocks drift.
Lamport clocks give an order consistent with causality.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Each process keeps counter C. Local event or send: C = C+1 (send carries C). Receive: C = max(C, msg) + 1. If event a happens-before b then C(a) < C(b); the converse is **not** true (equal or smaller timestamps do not prove concurrency). Vector clocks detect concurrency exactly.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: A: local=1, send m1=2. B: recv m1 → max(0,2)+1=3, send m2 → 4. C: recv m2 → max(0,4)+1=5. Final A=2, B=4, C=5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting +1 after max on receive.
- Believing C(a)<C(b) implies a→b.
- Mixing with wall-clock time.

activity.prompt: Simulate the events above and print final clocks as a dict in order A, B, C.
activity.hint: On receive take max then add 1.

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Quorum reads and writes

scenes.text: A key-value store keeps N=5 replicas and you must choose R and W.
R+W>N makes read and write sets overlap.

steps.title: Quorum rule
steps.body: With N replicas, a write succeeds after W acks and a read queries R replicas. If R+W>N, every read overlaps with the latest successful write (strong-ish consistency, ignoring edge cases like sloppy quorums). W=N gives fast reads but writes fail on any outage; R=1,W=1 favours availability and latency with eventual consistency.

steps.title: N=5
steps.body: R=3,W=3: 6>5 ✓ overlap. R=2,W=3: 5 is not >5 ✗ stale reads possible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking quorum alone gives linearizability.
- Ignoring clock/versioning for conflicts.
- Choosing W=N and expecting high availability.

activity.prompt: With N=5 replicas and write quorum W=3, what is the MINIMUM read quorum R that guarantees R+W>N?

quiz.why: At least one replica has the latest write.

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Consistent hashing

scenes.text: Adding a cache node with simple hash(key) % N remaps almost every key.
A hash ring moves only the keys of the neighbour.

steps.title: Ring
steps.body: Place nodes and keys on a circular hash space; a key belongs to the first node clockwise from its position. Adding/removing a node remaps only about 1/N of keys. Virtual nodes (many points per server) even out load. Used in Dynamo-style stores and caches.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using modulo hashing and suffering mass remapping.
- Few nodes without virtual nodes (hot spots).
- Forgetting wrap-around.

activity.prompt: Implement owner(k): the first node with position >= k (wrap to n1). Print owners for keys 5,25,45,75 as a list.
activity.hint: Walk nodes in position order; wrap at the end.

quiz.q: Consistent hashing moves on node add?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – availability of replicas

scenes.text: The CTO asks how much better three replicas are than one when each is 90% available.
Assuming independent failures, the service is down only if all replicas are down.

steps.title: Maths
steps.body: If each replica is up with probability a and failures are independent, the system with n replicas (any one suffices) has availability 1 − (1−a)^n. One replica: 0.90. Three: 1 − 0.1³ = 0.999. Caveat: real failures are correlated (same rack, same bug, same deploy), so use multiple zones. Serial dependencies multiply availability: 0.999 × 0.99 = 0.98901.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Put replicas in different availability zones and test failover regularly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming independence across one zone.
- Forgetting dependencies in series.
- Never testing failover.

activity.prompt: Print the availability of 3 independent replicas each 90% available (any one suffices).
activity.solution:
a=0.9;n=3
print(round(1-(1-a)**n,3))

courses.title: Machine Learning for MCA: Optimisation, Clustering, Validation
courses.summary: From-scratch practicals: gradient descent, the sigmoid/logistic model, k-means clustering and k-fold validation, with the maths shown. Related: uni-cse-ml, uni-cse-dl.
outcomes: Learners can run gradient descent steps by hand and in code
Learners can compute logistic probabilities

lessons.title: Lab: Gradient descent on a line

scenes.text: A model y = w·x must learn w from data where the true w is 2.
Each step moves w against the gradient of the mean squared error.

steps.title: Update
steps.body: Loss L(w) = (1/n)Σ(w·x−y)². Gradient dL/dw = (2/n)Σ(w·x−y)·x. Update w ← w − η·dL/dw with learning rate η. Too large η diverges; too small is slow. Features scaling helps convergence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong sign (ascending the loss).
- Learning rate too large.
- Forgetting to average over n.

activity.prompt: Run 3 steps of gradient descent (η=0.1, w=0) on x=[1,2,3], y=[2,4,6] and print the list of w after each step rounded to 4 decimals.
activity.solution:
x=[1,2,3];y=[2,4,6];w=0.0
out=[]
for _ in range(3):
    g=sum(2*(w*a-b)*a for a,b in zip(x,y))/len(x)
    w-=0.1*g
    out.append(round(w,4))
print(out)

lessons.title: Lab: Logistic regression probabilities

scenes.text: A model outputs a raw score of 2 for an email; the system needs a probability.
The sigmoid squashes any real number into (0,1).

steps.title: Model
steps.body: p = σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)) where z = w·x + b. σ(0)=0.5; σ(2)≈0.88. Classify with threshold 0.5 (z ≥ 0). Train by minimising cross-entropy loss −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)], which is convex. Coefficients are log-odds: e^w is the odds ratio change per unit.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: z=2 → p=0.88 → class 1. z=0 → 0.5, the decision boundary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using MSE for classification.
- Treating probability as certainty.
- Ignoring class imbalance when picking a threshold.

activity.prompt: Compute the sigmoid of z=2 rounded to 2 decimals and the predicted class with threshold 0.5. Print `0.88 1`.
activity.solution:
import math
z=2
p=1/(1+math.exp(-z))
print(f'{p:.2f}', int(p>=0.5))

lessons.title: Lab: k-means clustering

scenes.text: A retailer clusters customers by monthly spend: some spend little, some a lot.
k-means alternates assignment and centroid update.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Pick k initial centroids. Repeat: assign each point to the nearest centroid; recompute each centroid as the mean of its points; stop when assignments stop changing. Converges to a local optimum; results depend on initialisation (use k-means++ and multiple runs). Choose k with the elbow method or silhouette score. Scale features first.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Points [1,2,3,10,11,12], start centroids 1 and 12 → clusters {1,2,3} and {10,11,12} → centroids 2 and 11.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not scaling features.
- Assuming spherical equal-size clusters.
- Trusting a single random start.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – k-fold cross-validation report

scenes.text: A team compares two models and must report an honest estimate, not a lucky split.
K-fold averages performance over k different validation folds.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Split data into k folds; for each fold train on k−1 and validate on the held-out one; average the k scores and report mean ± standard deviation. Do all preprocessing (scaling, feature selection) inside each training fold to avoid **data leakage**. Keep a final untouched test set. Use stratified folds for imbalanced classes.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 5 folds with accuracies 0.80,0.90,0.70,0.85,0.75 → mean 0.80.

steps.title: Report
steps.body: Mean 0.80 with sd ≈ 0.07 means differences of 0.02 between models are not meaningful.

lessons.title: Lab: Run and list containers

scenes.text: Your team wants the web app in a container so it runs identically everywhere.
You start nginx and verify it.

steps.title: Core ideas
steps.body: An **image** is a read-only template; a **container** is a running instance with an isolated filesystem, process tree and network namespace, sharing the host kernel (unlike VMs). `docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx` runs detached and maps host 8080 to container 80. `docker ps` lists running containers.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: `docker ps` shows CONTAINER ID, IMAGE, STATUS, PORTS (0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp), NAMES.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting -p and wondering why the app is unreachable.
- Running as root unnecessarily.
- Storing data inside the container layer (lost on removal).

lessons.title: Lab: Debug a crashing container

scenes.text: The api container keeps restarting every few seconds.
Logs reveal a missing environment variable.

steps.title: Workflow
steps.body: `docker ps -a` shows exited containers and exit codes. `docker logs --tail 20 api` shows stdout/stderr. `docker inspect` shows config and env. `docker exec -it api sh` opens a shell in a running container. Fix by passing the variable with `-e` on a new run (containers are cattle: recreate instead of patching).

steps.title: Finding
steps.body: Log: `FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set` → exit code 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Editing files inside a container instead of the image.
- Ignoring exit codes (137 = killed, often out of memory).
- Restart policies hiding a crash loop.

lessons.title: Lab: Order Dockerfile layers for caching

scenes.text: Every code change reinstalls all dependencies, taking 4 minutes.
Layer order decides cache reuse.

steps.title: Cache rule
steps.body: Each instruction creates a layer; Docker reuses cached layers until one changes, then rebuilds all later layers. Put rarely changing steps first (base image, install dependencies from requirements file) and frequently changing steps last (COPY source). Use a small base image, a non-root USER and .dockerignore.

steps.title: Python app
steps.body: COPY requirements.txt → RUN pip install → COPY . . → CMD. Editing app code now reuses the pip layer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- COPY . . before installing dependencies.
- Putting secrets in layers (they stay in history).
- Huge base images.

activity.prompt: Order the Dockerfile instructions for the fastest rebuilds.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – fix a port conflict outage

scenes.text: A new container fails to start: port 8080 already allocated.
Find who owns the port, decide, then redeploy.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Error: `Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated`. Identify the owner with `docker ps` (another container) or host tools like `ss -ltnp`. Options: stop the old container if it is the previous version, or map a different host port. Always confirm what the old container is before stopping it.

steps.title: Case
steps.body: Old container web-old (previous release) holds 8080. Stop and remove it, run the new one, verify with docker ps.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Use unique ports per service, a reverse proxy, and compose files so ports are documented.

courses.title: Applied Cyber Security (Defensive) Lab
courses.summary: Defensive security practicals: password entropy and hashing, log analysis for brute-force attempts, threat modelling with STRIDE and a hardening checklist. Foundations: uni-cse-security. Educational and defensive only.
outcomes: Learners can estimate password strength with entropy

lessons.title: Lab: Password entropy

scenes.text: A campus portal was breached because users picked short passwords.
Entropy estimates how many guesses an attacker needs.

steps.title: Entropy
steps.body: For a random password of length L from an alphabet of size N, entropy = L·log2(N) bits. 8 characters from 62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9): 8·5.95 ≈ 47.6 bits. Human-chosen passwords have far less entropy than this formula says because people use words and patterns. Length beats complexity: 12 random lowercase letters gives 56.4 bits. Use a password manager and MFA.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Random 8 from 62 chars ≈ 47.6 bits; random 12 from 26 chars ≈ 56.4 bits.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the formula to non-random choices like 'Password@1'.
- Reusing passwords across sites.
- Relying on forced symbol rules instead of length.

activity.prompt: Print the entropy in bits (1 decimal) of a random 8-character password over 62 symbols.
activity.solution:
import math
print(round(8*math.log2(62),1))

quiz.q: Which adds more entropy for random passwords?
Best defence along with strong passwords?

lessons.title: Lab: Salted password hashing

scenes.text: A startup's user table leaks; passwords were stored as plain SHA-256.
Salting and slow hashes make mass cracking expensive.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Never store plain or reversibly encrypted passwords. Use a slow, memory-hard password hash (Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt) with a unique random salt per user. A salt stops identical passwords having identical hashes and defeats precomputed rainbow tables. Plain fast hashes such as SHA-256 allow billions of guesses per second on GPUs. Compare in constant time. Python's hashlib shows the idea; production code uses a vetted library.

steps.title: Same password, different salts
steps.body: sha256('password123') starts ef92b778; sha256('salt9'+'password123') starts 38860e68 — completely different.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using MD5/SHA-1/plain SHA-256 for passwords.
- A single global salt.
- Rolling your own scheme.

activity.prompt: Print the first 8 hex digits of sha256('password123'), then of sha256('salt9password123'), separated by a space.
activity.solution:
import hashlib
a=hashlib.sha256(b'password123').hexdigest()[:8]
b=hashlib.sha256(b'salt9password123').hexdigest()[:8]
print(a,b)

Response: block the IP at the firewall, require key-based SSH, disable password login and root login, add fail2ban/rate limiting and MFA, and review for any 'Accepted password' from that IP (possible compromise). steps.title: STRIDE

Information disclosure → encryption, access control. Denial of service → rate limits, redundancy. Elevation of privilege → least privilege, authorisation checks. lessons.title: Lab: From topic to research question

scenes.text: Ritu says: 'I will study machine learning.' Her guide asks: what exactly?
A good question is specific, answerable with data and novel enough.

steps.title: Criteria
steps.body: FINER: Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant. A research question names the population, intervention/method, comparison and outcome. A hypothesis is a falsifiable statement ('Model A achieves higher F1 than baseline B on dataset D'). Null hypothesis H0: no difference.

steps.title: Refine
steps.body: Vague: 'ML in healthcare.' Better: 'Does gradient boosting predict 30-day readmission with higher AUC than logistic regression on the public MIMIC-style dataset?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Question too broad.
- Unfalsifiable hypotheses.
- Choosing the method before the question.

activity.prompt: Sort each statement into a good research question/hypothesis or a weak one.

items.text: Does adding data augmentation raise test accuracy of a CNN on dataset X by at least 2 points?

lessons.title: Lab: Sample size for a survey

scenes.text: You must survey students about placement stress and want a ±5% margin at 95% confidence.
Cochran's formula gives the sample size.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: n = z²·p(1−p) / e². For 95% confidence z=1.96; with unknown proportion use p=0.5 (worst case); e=0.05. n = 3.8416·0.25/0.0025 = 384.16 → round **up** to 385. For a finite population N, adjust n' = n / (1 + (n−1)/N). Random sampling matters more than size: a huge biased sample is still biased.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding down.
- Convenience sampling presented as random.
- Ignoring non-response bias.

activity.prompt: Using z=1.96, p=0.5 and margin of error 0.05, what is the minimum sample size (round up)?

sources: Standard undergraduate computing syllabus topics (original explanation)

lessons.title: Lab: Descriptive statistics and confidence interval

scenes.text: Five pilot users rated a tool 4,5,6,7,8 out of 10.
Mean and spread summarise; an interval conveys uncertainty.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Mean x̄ = Σx/n. Sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1)). Standard error = s/√n. Approximate 95% CI for a mean (large n): x̄ ± 1.96·SE; for small samples use the t-distribution (wider). Report effect size and CI, not just p-values. A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if H0 were true — not the probability H0 is true.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by n instead of n−1 for sample sd.
- Interpreting p<0.05 as 'proven'.
- Using the normal approximation with tiny n.

steps.title: Conventions
steps.body: Resources are nouns: /orders, /orders/42. Verbs: GET read (safe, idempotent), POST create, PUT replace (idempotent), PATCH partial update, DELETE remove (idempotent). Codes: 200 OK, 201 Created (+Location header), 204 No Content, 400 bad input, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 429 too many requests, 500 server error. Version the API (/v1).

lessons.title: Lab: Pagination

scenes.text: GET /orders returns 2 million rows and times out.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: Offset pagination: `?limit=10&offset=20` — simple, but slow on large offsets and unstable if rows are inserted. Cursor (keyset) pagination: `?after=<last_id>&limit=10` — fast, stable. Return total or next link. Cap limit server-side (e.g. max 100). Sort deterministically.

steps.title: Worked example

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No maximum limit.
- Non-deterministic sort order.
- Using offset for infinite scroll on big tables.

lessons.title: Lab: Idempotency keys for payments

scenes.text: A mobile app retried POST /payments after a timeout and charged a customer twice.
An idempotency key makes the retry safe.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Client sends a unique Idempotency-Key header per logical operation. Server stores (key → result); on a repeat it returns the stored result instead of repeating the effect. Keys expire after a window (e.g. 24 h). Combine with database unique constraints. Networks fail in ambiguous ways (request lost vs response lost), so clients retry; servers must tolerate it.

steps.title: Flow
steps.body: First request with key k1: charge ₹500, store. Retry with k1: return the same receipt, no new charge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Generating a new key per retry.
- Storing the key after the side effect without a transaction.
- Using idempotency keys for GET.

a.text: The payment API timed out; the mobile app is unsure whether the charge happened. What should the app do?

choices.label: Resend POST with a brand-new key
Resend the same request with the same Idempotency-Key
Tell the user to try again later without checking

bad.text: The customer is charged twice and raises a dispute.

bad2.text: Support tickets pile up for ghost charges.

good.text: Exactly one charge, a consistent receipt, happy customer.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – token-bucket rate limiter

scenes.text: One client sends bursts that slow the API for everyone.
A token bucket allows bursts but limits the average rate.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Bucket capacity C holds tokens; refill r tokens per second (up to C). Each request consumes one token; if none are available return 429 with a Retry-After header. Allows bursts up to C, long-run rate r. Store per client (user id/API key/IP) in Redis for multi-server setups. Alternatives: fixed window (boundary bursts), sliding window.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: C=3, r=1/s. Requests at t = 0,0,0,0,1,1.5,2 → ok,ok,ok,deny,ok,deny,ok.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Per-server counters behind a load balancer.
- Rate limiting only by IP (NAT).
- No Retry-After header.

activity.hint: Refill by elapsed time, then consume one token.

lessons.title: Lab: Back-of-envelope estimation

scenes.text: A startup expects 10 million users posting 2 photo captions of ~1 KB per day.
The CTO wants yearly storage before choosing a database.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: State assumptions, convert to per-second and per-day numbers, and round sensibly. Useful constants: 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s; 1 KB ≈ 10³ B; 1 TB = 10¹² B (decimal). Writes/s = writes/day ÷ 86,400. Peak is often 2–5× average. Estimation checks feasibility, not exactness.

steps.title: Calc
steps.body: 10M × 2 = 20M posts/day × 1 KB = 20 GB/day. Per year: 20 × 365 = 7,300 GB = 7.3 TB (before replication ×3 ≈ 21.9 TB). Writes/s ≈ 20M/86,400 ≈ 231.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing bits and bytes.
- Forgetting replication and indexes.
- Using average load for peak capacity.

activity.prompt: Compute yearly storage in TB (decimal, 365 days) for 10 million users × 2 posts/day × 1 KB (1 KB = 1000 B). Print `7.3`.
activity.solution:
users=10_000_000
bytes_year=users*2*1000*365
print(round(bytes_year/1e12,1))

options: Peak is often several times average

lessons.title: Lab: Cache hit ratio and latency

scenes.text: Each product page hits the database in 50 ms; a cache answers in 1 ms.
Effective latency depends on the hit ratio.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: Effective latency = h·t_cache + (1−h)·t_miss (miss path includes cache lookup + DB; simplified here). With h=0.9: 0.9·1 + 0.1·50 = 5.9 ms. Raising h to 0.99 gives 1.49 ms. Strategies: cache-aside (app loads on miss), write-through, write-back; TTLs and invalidation are the hard part. Beware cache stampede on expiry (use locking or jittered TTLs).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: h=0.9 → 5.9 ms average, a 8.5× speed-up over 50 ms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Caching without an invalidation plan.
- Caching user-specific data under a shared key.
- Ignoring stampedes.

lessons.title: Lab: Remove single points of failure

scenes.text: The app runs on one server behind no load balancer; a disk failure took the site down for 3 hours.
The fix is redundancy at every tier.

steps.title: Checklist
steps.body: Load balancer (itself redundant) → multiple stateless app servers across zones → replicated database with automatic failover → shared object storage for files → redundant DNS. Make app servers stateless (sessions in a store like Redis). Health checks remove bad nodes. Test failure drills regularly. Load-balancing algorithms: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing for caches.

steps.title: Finding
steps.body: Single DB primary = SPOF; add a synchronous or semi-synchronous replica with automated promotion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A load balancer that is itself single.
- Storing sessions in app memory.
- Untested failover.

a.text: Post-mortem: single app server, single DB. You have budget for one improvement this month. Which gives the best resilience gain?

choices.label: Bigger server
choices.feedback: Still a single point of failure.

choices.label: Two stateless app servers behind a load balancer and a DB replica with failover

bad.text: The next failure again means a full outage.

good.text: The next node failure is invisible to users; you schedule failover drills.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – URL shortener IDs

scenes.text: A campus club wants short.example.com/abc links for 1 billion URLs.
Base62 encoding of an auto-increment or distributed ID gives short strings.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: API: POST /shorten {url} → code; GET /{code} → 301/302 redirect. Store (id, long_url, created, expiry). Generate id with a distributed counter or Snowflake-style IDs, then Base62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z) encode. 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, so 7 characters suffice for billions. Cache hot links; reads dominate (read:write ≈ 100:1). Use 302 if you need click analytics; 301 is cached by browsers. Validate URLs to prevent abuse.

steps.title: Hash alternative
steps.body: Hashing the URL risks collisions and needs retries; counters avoid collisions but need coordination.

activity.prompt: Implement base62(n) using the alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z and print base62(125).
activity.solution:
A='0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ'
def base62(n):
    if n==0: return A[0]
    s=''
    while n:
        n,r=divmod(n,62); s=A[r]+s
    return s
print(base62(125))

lessons.title: Lab: Write an architecture decision record

scenes.text: The team argues for three weeks about PostgreSQL versus MongoDB for the project.
An ADR ends the debate with recorded reasons.

steps.title: ADR format
steps.body: Title, Status (proposed/accepted/superseded), Context (forces and constraints), Decision, Consequences (good and bad), Alternatives considered. Short, dated, stored in the repository. Decisions rely on requirements: transactions and relational reports favour PostgreSQL; flexible nested documents and rapid schema change may favour MongoDB. Name the trade-off you accept.

steps.title: Decision
steps.body: 'Use PostgreSQL 16 because issue/return requires multi-row transactions and reporting joins; accept less flexible schema changes.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing by hype.
- No alternatives listed.
- Not revisiting when context changes.

lessons.title: Lab: Capacity with Little's law

scenes.text: The demo API receives 50 requests per second and each takes 0.2 s on average.
How many requests are in flight at once?

steps.title: Little's law
steps.body: L = λ·W: average number in the system = arrival rate × average time in system. 50 req/s × 0.2 s = 10 concurrent requests. If your server pool handles 8 concurrent requests, queues grow without bound. Capacity plan: concurrency needed = rate × latency; add headroom (target ≤ 60–70% utilisation).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: If latency rises to 1 s under load, concurrency = 50, a hidden cause of cascading failure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring that latency rises with load.
- Sizing for average rather than peak.
- Mixing units (ms vs s).

lessons.title: Lab: Order a CI/CD pipeline

scenes.text: A broken build reached production on Friday evening.
The pipeline needs gates in the right order.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body: Commit → build and lint → unit tests → static analysis/security scan (dependency check, secrets scan) → package artefact once → deploy to staging → integration/end-to-end tests → manual or automated approval → deploy to production with canary/blue-green → monitor and auto-rollback. Principle: build once, promote the same artefact.

steps.title: Fail fast
steps.body: Cheap checks (lint, unit tests) run first so failures cost minutes, not hours.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rebuilding a different artefact per environment.
- Skipping security scans.
- No rollback plan.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – viva and defence readiness

scenes.text: The external examiner asks: 'What is novel here, and what would you do differently?'
Evidence and honesty beat jargon.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.body: One-sentence contribution; problem statement; related work and gap; architecture and key decision (ADR); evaluation results with baselines and limits; threats to validity; ethical and security considerations; reproducibility (repo, seeds, instructions); what you would do next. Rehearse a 15-minute talk and a Q&A with two peers; prepare for 'why not X?' questions.

steps.title: Answer shape
steps.body: 'We chose X over Y because of Z; the cost was W, and our evaluation shows the trade-off clearly in Table 3.'

steps.title: Own it
steps.body: Be able to explain every line and every number; admit what you did not test.
